doc.title: Eddie Bert interviewed by Monk Rowe, Danbury, Connecticut, November 20, 2001

title: Meeting Charles Mingus and how he taught his music
summary: Meeting Mingus in San Francisco, Debut recordings, and learning tunes by rote.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Playing with and understanding Thelonious Monk

blocks.x: Good. Tell me about, if you would, the Charles Mingus Jazz Workshop.

Well I met Charles when I was with Benny Goodman the first time. We were in San Francisco and Clyde Lombardi, the bass player with Red, you know Red’s small band, well we were with Benny at the time. Yeah it was Benny’s band. Clyde was on Benny’s band. And he said, “there’s a bass player I want to hear down in the International Quarter.” I said, “okay, I’ll go with you.” So we went. They had four basses and drums. Right? And Mingus is playing lead bass. So that’s how I met him. And the next time I heard of him he had joined Red’s trio in 1950 and they were going back to play The Embers. He had been in California. Tal Farlow and Mingus. So anyway Mingus got established in New York and he started this workshop. He and Teo Macero. And we used to rehearse quite a bit. And it was all original material. And eventually — I’m shortening it — Mingus got his own thing. I did an album with him at The Bohemia. It was me, George Barrow, Mal Waldron and Willie Jones. It was in ’55. And Debut, eventually, I mean they put it out but it eventually got to Atlantic and went to a whole bunch of different albums. It was put out many times.
Kind of piecemeal, or under different titles?

Yeah. And eventually Fantasy put out an eleven CD album of all the Debut stuff. And it said, I had read a review and they said there was eleven tracks that were never issued of The Bohemia stuff. So I called Fantasy Records and I said, “can you send me a cassette of the eleven tracks?” “Oh no, we can’t break up the — you know, you’ve got to buy the whole thing.” So I said, “well I’m on it, can you do anything?” So they said, “well we’ll give it to you for five dollars a CD.” So I said okay. It came to sixty bucks. I wanted to hear some of the stuff from Debut anyway. So I got the thing, and I looked up what I made for the date. Sixty bucks.
That’s very interesting. Did he have a certain amount of — I should rephrase that — did he require some things from his sidemen that other leaders wouldn’t?

Well yeah. I mean he wanted you to play his music. And the way you played his music with a small group, he didn’t write it out. You go up to his apartment and he’d play it for you on the piano, and you’d learn it in your head. And that’s how you learned it. Because he said, “if I write it out you’re going to play it different,” which you do. If it’s written out you play it different. But if you get it in your head and you play it like you want to play it. And he says, “play it your way.” He didn’t say any specific thing. Here it is. Like for instance “Jump Monk.” When I first learned that, it was by rote. I just learned it. And when we went on The Bohemia, there was no music.
And he’d change things during the night, you know change little things. You’d be playing and he’s singing in your ear, “play this,” and he’s singing. So you play it as he’s singing it.
You had to be on your toes.
Gosh. Very interesting. Did they ever record, was it the Town Hall concert or something?
